summary: Presents Operations, Administration, and Maintenance requirements for TRILL networks, covering the functions and tools needed to monitor and troubleshoot them. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6905 lists the checks and measurements that operations tools for TRILL networks should support. It sets requirements for protocol designers rather than defining a protocol.

subtitle: The operational and maintenance functions required for TRILL networks

tldr.problem: Operators need ways to check reachability, detect failures, trace paths, and measure TRILL network performance. The RFC sets common requirements for those tools.
tldr.mechanism: It specifies requirements for OAM between Routing Bridges, including connectivity and continuity checks, path tracing, performance monitoring, and security controls.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6905 is an informational requirements document. It does not define an OAM protocol.

facts.label: Required framework
facts.value: One extensible framework for the OAM functions in scope

sections.title: Scope of TRILL Operations and Maintenance
sections.content:
Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) covers tools for monitoring and troubleshooting networks. This document applies to OAM between Routing Bridges (RBridges) in a TRILL campus, over links selected by TRILL routing.

The requirements address proactive fault monitoring and faster diagnosis of defects or failures. The RFC assumes familiarity with OAM concepts from other standards and does not redefine them.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC describes what monitoring and troubleshooting tools for TRILL should do. Its scope is the links between Routing Bridges inside a TRILL campus.

sections.title: Connectivity, Continuity, and Path Tracing
sections.content:
OAM frames normally follow the path selected by TRILL. It MUST also be possible to make them follow the path of a specified flow. OAM frames must stay within the TRILL campus and must be identifiable for OAM processing.

OAM must check connectivity between any two RBridges and along a specified flow path. It must support connectivity checks for distribution trees. Continuity checks periodically test whether RBridges remain reachable, while path tracing shows the route for a specified unicast flow; tracing all selectable least-cost paths is a SHOULD-level requirement.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators need to test whether two RBridges can reach each other and whether that remains true over time. They also need to trace the route used by a specified flow.

sections.title: Performance Measurements
sections.content:
The RFC says OAM SHOULD measure packet-loss statistics for a flow end to end, over a path section, and across all least-cost paths. Measurements may be proactive or started on demand.

OAM SHOULD measure two-way delay between RBridges. It MAY measure one-way delay for a specified flow, including over a path section. OAM MAY also report how packets are distributed across equal-cost next hops.
sections.plainLanguage: OAM measurements can show packet loss and delay across a route or part of it. The RFC requires a capability for two-way delay measurement at the SHOULD level.

sections.title: A Shared, Extensible OAM Framework
sections.content:
All TRILL OAM functions in scope MUST use a single OAM framework. The framework MUST support extensions, with a version number and flexible information elements such as Type-Length-Value (TLV) structures. OAM functions must be able to run at the same time without interfering with one another.

Connectivity and continuity checks must be available on demand or proactively. Related errors and operational counters must be accessible to network management applications, such as through SNMP. Reuse of existing OAM standards is recommended where practical.
sections.plainLanguage: TRILL OAM functions should share one framework that can be extended. Multiple checks should be able to run together, and their results should be available to management tools.

sections.title: Security and Fault Reporting
sections.content:
Implementations MUST protect OAM against security and denial-of-service attacks. They must prevent OAM messages from causing congestion, restrict access to sensitive topology information, and keep OAM packets within the TRILL campus. Shaping or rate limiting is recommended for frequently generated messages.

OAM MUST provide a fault-indication framework and allow different fault indications to be enabled or disabled. A defect-detection and indication framework is recommended, including configurable thresholds, logging, and possible remote notification.
sections.plainLanguage: OAM tools must not expose network details to unauthorized users or let diagnostic traffic overwhelm the network. They must also provide ways to report faults.
